title: Sleep and memory
passage:
Researchers recruited 60 college students and taught all of them a list of 40 word pairs at 9 p.m. Participants were then randomly assigned to one of two groups. The sleep group went home and slept normally. The wake group stayed in the lab overnight under supervision and was not allowed to sleep. Both groups were tested on the word pairs at 9 a.m. the next morning (Test 1).

To check whether tiredness alone explained the results, both groups were allowed a full night of recovery sleep and tested again 48 hours after learning (Test 2). Neither group studied the words between tests.
cap: Table 1. Mean percentage of word pairs correctly recalled.

qs.q: What is the independent variable in this study?
qs.a: Whether participants slept the night after learning
w: The percentage of word pairs each group recalled
The number of word pairs each participant learned
The time of morning when the first test was given
qs.e: The researchers manipulated sleep versus wakefulness by random assignment. Recall is the dependent variable they measured.

qs.q: Why did the researchers include Test 2?
qs.a: To rule out that the wake group did worse only because it was tired at Test 1
w: To measure how quickly participants could learn a second set of word pairs
To give the sleep group a second chance to learn pairs they had missed
To confirm that random assignment had produced groups of equal ability
qs.e: After recovery sleep, the wake group was no longer sleep-deprived but still recalled less, which suggests the original sleep helped store the memories.

qs.q: Which conclusion do the results best support?
qs.a: Sleep soon after learning helps consolidate new declarative memories
w: Sleep deprivation permanently damages the hippocampus
Recall improves the more often a word list is tested
Sleep has no effect on memory once people have recovered
qs.e: The sleep group's advantage held at Test 2, which fits the idea that sleep, especially slow-wave sleep, helps move new memories into long-term storage.

qs.q: Because participants were randomly assigned to groups, the researchers can more reasonably claim:
qs.a: That sleep caused the difference in recall
w: That the results apply to all ages
That the effect is the same in every culture
That participants could not guess the hypothesis
qs.e: Random assignment spreads other differences evenly across groups, which supports causal conclusions (internal validity). Generalizing beyond college students is a question of external validity.

title: Who helps in an emergency?
passage:
Participants sat alone in booths and talked with other 'participants' over an intercom. In reality, the other voices were recordings. Partway through, one voice appeared to have a seizure and called for help. The researchers varied how many other people the participant believed were listening: none, one or four. They recorded whether the participant left the booth to get help before the recording ended, and how long it took.

Afterward, every participant was told about the deception and why it was needed, and was given the chance to withdraw their data.

qs.q: Which concept best explains the pattern in Table 1?
qs.a: Diffusion of responsibility
w: Social facilitation
Group polarization
Cognitive dissonance
qs.e: Each person feels less personally responsible when others could also act, so helping drops and slows as the group grows. This is the bystander effect.

qs.q: What was the dependent variable?
qs.a: Whether and how quickly participants sought help
w: The number of other people the participant believed were present
The content and length of the recorded seizure
Whether or not participants were deceived about the setup
qs.e: The researchers manipulated group size (the independent variable) and measured helping.

qs.q: Telling participants about the deception afterward is an example of:
qs.a: Debriefing
w: Informed consent
Random assignment
A double-blind procedure
qs.e: When deception is necessary, ethical guidelines require debriefing: explaining the true purpose after participation.

qs.q: If the other listeners were the participant's close friends instead of strangers, helping would most likely:
qs.a: Increase, because friends feel more responsible for one another and share clearer norms
w: Decrease further, because responsibility would be spread across more trusted people
Stay the same, because the number of listeners would not change at all
Drop to zero, because each friend would wait for another friend to act first
qs.e: The bystander effect is weaker among people who know each other. Group cohesion and shared norms make it easier to act.

title: Neighborhood income and diabetes
passage:
A public health team surveyed 12,000 adults across a large city. Neighborhoods were sorted into five groups (quintiles) by median household income, from Q1 (lowest) to Q5 (highest). The team recorded the percentage of adults with diagnosed type 2 diabetes and the distance from each home to the nearest full-service grocery store.

The team noted that lower-income neighborhoods also had fewer parks and more fast-food outlets per resident. A city council member proposed opening a subsidized grocery store in each Q1 neighborhood.
cap: Table 1. Diabetes prevalence and grocery access by income quintile.

qs.q: The step-by-step decline in diabetes across all five quintiles best illustrates:
qs.a: The social gradient in health
w: Absolute poverty
Upward social mobility
The demographic transition
qs.e: Health improves at each step up the income ladder, not only between the poorest and everyone else.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by this study?
qs.a: Grocery distance and income are associated with diabetes, but causation isn't shown
w: Living far from a grocery store causes type 2 diabetes in adults of every income level
Opening a grocery store in each Q1 neighborhood will cut diabetes there by about half
Income is related to grocery access, but it has no relationship with diabetes rates
qs.e: This is a cross-sectional, observational study. Other factors that vary with income, such as parks, fast food, health care and stress, could explain the link.

qs.q: A conflict theorist would most likely explain these findings in terms of:
qs.a: Unequal distribution of resources between more and less powerful groups
w: How the health care system helps keep society stable and orderly
The shared meanings residents attach to food and eating habits
Individual lifestyle choices made independently of social forces
qs.e: Conflict theory focuses on how inequality in power and resources shapes outcomes such as access to healthy food.

qs.q: Lower-income neighborhoods in the study had fewer parks AND more fast-food outlets. For the council member's proposal, this suggests that:
qs.a: A grocery store alone may not fully cut diabetes, since several factors differ
w: The grocery store will definitely work, because access is the main cause of diabetes
Parks should be removed from the analysis, because they don't affect health at all
Fast-food outlets likely lower diabetes rates, because they offer convenient meals
qs.e: Several social determinants of health vary together, so changing just one may have a limited effect.

title: Cues and relapse
passage:
Rats were trained to press a lever that delivered a dose of cocaine. Each dose was paired with a light and a tone. After rats pressed reliably, researchers began an extinction phase: lever presses no longer delivered cocaine, the light or the tone. Pressing gradually dropped to near zero over two weeks.

In the test phase, some rats were exposed to the light and tone alone, without cocaine, and their lever pressing jumped back up for a short time. Another group received the test after a three-week break with no training and also pressed more than they had at the end of extinction.

Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake in brain reward pathways, including the nucleus accumbens.

qs.q: During training, the light and tone served as:
qs.a: Conditioned stimuli
w: Unconditioned stimuli
Unconditioned responses
Negative reinforcers
qs.e: They were neutral at first but became meaningful by being paired with cocaine, the unconditioned stimulus.

qs.q: Lever pressing during training increased because cocaine acted as:
qs.a: A positive reinforcer
w: A negative reinforcer
A positive punisher
A conditioned stimulus
qs.e: Something desirable was added after the behavior, making the behavior more likely. That's positive reinforcement in operant conditioning.

qs.q: The rise in pressing after the three-week break with no training is best described as:
qs.a: Spontaneous recovery
w: Stimulus generalization
Acquisition
Habituation
qs.e: After extinction, a response can return after time passes. This shows extinction suppresses rather than erases learning.

qs.q: Cocaine's effect on dopamine most directly:
qs.a: Raises synaptic dopamine, strengthening the behavior's rewarding effect
w: Lowers dopamine in the synapse, which the brain experiences as a craving
Blocks dopamine receptors, which makes natural rewards feel less pleasant
Speeds dopamine breakdown, which shortens each burst of reward signaling
qs.e: Blocking reuptake leaves dopamine in the synapse longer, which drives reward signaling in the mesolimbic pathway.

title: Test instructions and performance
passage:
Women majoring in science were randomly assigned to take the same difficult 20-question math test under one of two instructions. In the 'diagnostic' condition, they were told the test had shown gender differences in the past. In the 'neutral' condition, they were told the test had never shown gender differences. A comparison group of men received the diagnostic instructions.

After the test, participants rated how anxious they felt during it.
cap: Table 1. Test scores and self-rated anxiety.

qs.q: Which phenomenon do these results best demonstrate?
qs.a: Stereotype threat
w: The self-serving bias
The overjustification effect
The halo effect
qs.e: Reminding women of a negative stereotype about their group lowered their scores. With neutral instructions, they performed as well as men.

qs.q: Why is the 'women, neutral' condition important to the study's design?
qs.a: It shows how women score when the stereotype isn't raised, isolating the instructions' effect
w: It controls for differences in overall math ability between women and men
It shows that men's scores do not depend on the instructions they are given
It makes the test easier, so it serves as a baseline for the hardest version
qs.e: Comparing women under the two instructions, with random assignment, isolates the effect of the instructions.

qs.q: The anxiety ratings suggest that the effect on scores may work through:
qs.a: Heightened anxiety that interferes with performance
w: Lower motivation to finish all of the test
A real difference in underlying math ability
Less time available to complete the questions
qs.e: Anxiety was highest in the group that scored lowest, which points to anxiety as a possible mediator. The study doesn't prove this, because anxiety was measured, not manipulated.

qs.q: Which change would most improve the study's external validity?
qs.a: Repeating it with women from many backgrounds and fields, not just science
w: Using a shorter test so participants don't get tired before the end
Removing the men's group so the study focuses only on women
Telling participants the hypothesis so they understand the purpose
qs.e: External validity is about generalizing beyond this sample and setting. A broader sample would show whether the effect holds more widely.
